notes: B. oleracea belongs to the close rapa/oleracea lineage but retains the canonical Brassicaceae tetradynamous androecium with four long and two short fertile stamens. Close phylogenetic proximity cannot satisfy the frozen absence gate.
B. napus carries the B. rapa genome contribution but remains tetradynamous with four long and two short stamens. The derived allopolyploid relationship is not used to rescue a failed morphology gate.

Classical cpDNA systematics place D. erucoides among the closest apparent relatives of the B. rapa/B. oleracea lineage. Species morphology directly records four long central and two short lateral stamens, so it fails before ecological eligibility matters.

Raphanus is closely related to the rapa/oleracea lineage. Direct pollination experiments show effective insect pollination, but the same source explicitly records four long and two short tetradynamous stamens; therefore this high-quality ecological candidate is still ineligible as a negative-architecture control.

Nikolov directly documents six stamens of approximately equal height in S. elata. Cullen & Ashman sampled five natural S. elata populations and report Stanleyoid species as generalist insect-pollinated with visits from large-bodied bees and wasps. However, equal/nearly equal stamens also occur in other Brassicaceae lineages; no frozen common phylogenetic surface has established S. elata as the closest eligible negative-architecture taxon after the Brassiceae candidates fail.

The sampled New World Thelypodieae group containing S. pinnata is described as sharing stamens of nearly equal length. Cullen & Ashman sampled S. pinnata populations and report Stanleyoid generalist insect pollination. This supplies a second biologically eligible family-level candidate, so source quality alone cannot be used to pretend that the closest eligible phylogenetic control is known.
